questions.q: What does a SAST (Static Application Security Testing) tool actually analyze?
options: Live network traffic between the application and its database
The source code itself, for known-dangerous patterns, without ever executing the application
Only the third-party packages a project depends on
User behavior logs collected after deployment
questions.explain: SAST reads source code and matches it against known-dangerous patterns, which is exactly why it never needs to execute the application to run.

questions.q: Why is SAST well-suited to run on every single commit, as described in this lesson?
options: Because it only runs once a year during a scheduled audit
Because it requires a full staging environment with a live database
Because it needs manual review before every run
Because it doesn't execute the application, so it's cheap and fast enough to run on every pull request's diff
questions.explain: Since SAST never starts the application, it can run in seconds against just the changed code, making it cheap enough for every commit.

questions.q: What problem does dependency scanning (software composition analysis) solve that SAST does not?
options: It checks the exact versions of third-party packages a project imports against known-vulnerability databases, covering code the team never wrote
It replaces the need to ever run automated tests
It tests the running application from the outside with real HTTP requests
It only checks for hardcoded secrets in source code
questions.explain: SAST only looks at code the team wrote; dependency scanning checks the versions of imported third-party packages against public vulnerability databases.

questions.q: In the GitHub Actions workflow shown in this lesson, at what point do the Bandit and pip-audit steps run relative to deployment?
options: After the application has already been deployed to production
Only during a manual penetration test, separate from CI
Before the application is built into a deployable artifact or deployed anywhere, on every pull request
Only once per quarter, regardless of how often code changes
questions.explain: Both steps run on pull requests, before the application is built into a deployable artifact — the earliest and cheapest checks in the pipeline.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about the output of SAST and dependency-scanning tools?
options: Every finding from either tool is a confirmed exploit that must block the build
These tools never produce false positives, so no triage is ever needed
Neither tool is perfect — some findings are false positives, so teams need a habit of triaging quickly rather than ignoring or over-blocking on every finding
Their output cannot be reviewed until a human manually re-runs the scan
questions.explain: The lesson notes both tools can produce false positives, and that effective teams triage findings rather than ignoring them or treating every one as a hard blocker.
